newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Sao Paulo on track to elect its first black mayor.
newsitem.headline: Sao Paulo on track to elect its first black mayor.

text.p: If the polls prove right, Sao Paulo, Brazil's largest city, will elect its first black mayor on Friday in the second round of nationwide municipal elections.

Celso Pitta, a Harvard-educated accountant who has never before run for political office, enjoys a 19 percentage point lead in pre-election polls over his opponent, former Sao Paulo mayor Luiza Erundina.

A Pitta victory would shatter a long-held view that Sao Paulo's 6.7 million voters would never elect a black to the mayor's office, although blacks and mixed-race people represent more than half the city's electorate.

"It would change the image of blacks in politics and represent a huge boost to the black population's self-esteem," said Jose Roberto da Degolacao, a sociologist who leads a black action group that supports Pitta's candidacy.

Despite this considerable accomplishment, Pitta has not used the race card to promote his candidacy. On the contrary, analysts say he has downplayed race for fear of alienating middle-class whites, who represent the bulk of his support.
Newspapers reported Pitta aides have even turned down endorsement offers from prominent black activists such as former Brazilian soccer star Pele and U.S. civil rights leader Jesse Jackson.
Pitta claims race should play no part in politics. "When I decided to run for office, I didn't paint my face black," he told reporters.
Analysts said Pitta's success has very little to do with the colour of his skin but is directly tied to the popularity of his political godfather, incumbent mayor Paulo Maluf.
A failed two-time presidential candidate, Maluf hand picked Pitta to lead his right-wing PPB party's ticket in the Sao Paulo mayoral race.

Throughout the campaign, Maluf has been a constant presence with Pitta and the message to the voters has been that Pitta will continue Maluf's busy civil-works administration. That is also the thrust of his campaign slogan: "Vote for Pitta -- because Sao Paulo cannot afford to stop."
The son of a car salesman and a ranking civil servant, the 50 year-old Pitta has rarely suffered the privations and discrimination that is routine for most Brazilian blacks.
He studied at a private high school, completed post graduate degrees in Great Britain and the United States and rarely moved outside a middle-class environment.
